survey: A cluster of coral on a rock base, viewed from the front on a flat seabed. A large dark purple-grey rock sits in the center, with smaller grey-green stones around it on the left and right. A tall pink branching coral grows from behind and on top of the center rock. Its trunk splits into rounded, forked branches that fan upward and keep roughly even thickness. An orange branching coral stands behind on the left and a smaller one behind on the right; both rise from behind the rocks. A violet-pink coral with rounded lobes grows at the front left, rooted where the small left stones meet the large rock. A small red fan-shaped coral sits at the front center, its base resting on the seabed against the foot of the rock. Every coral has a visible or hidden base in the rocks, and the rocks rest on the seabed with contact shadows. Nothing floats. Branches overlap in depth but do not pass through or melt into each other. As a natural object, the coral has no counts or joints that must be exact. The forms are simplified but believable.
